# R4 Digest — Saul Made King + Address (6651–8140)
**Source:** Tsumura, *The First Book of Samuel* (NICOT, 2006)
**Reader:** extraction subagent R4
**Coverage:** slice `R4_saul_king_address_6651-8140.txt` read in full (raw **6651–8140** ≈ commentary pp. 262–330: III. Story of Saul 9:1–15:35 open; A. Saul Made King 9:1–11:15; B. Samuel’s Address 12:1–25). No reading beyond range.

## Claims

### C-R4-01 | Section frame: “Story of Saul” and narrative retardation
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** After ch. 8 the reader expects how Samuel chooses a king; instead the narrative introduces young Saul seeking lost asses. This retardation heightens expectation. Saul seems occupied only with farm matters and seemingly does not know Samuel, but God sees these events as crucial and was “clearly guiding by his providence the whole business of choosing the requested king.”
- **Quote:** “while the fate of the nation hangs in balance, the reader is introduced to a story of a young man named Saul who is looking for lost asses. This retardation of the narrative heightens the expectation. … He was clearly guiding by his providence the whole business of choosing the requested king.”
- **Locus:** p. 262 / slice L1–5; opening of III. “Story of Saul” (9:1–15:35)
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[divine-providence]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R4-02 | Kish’s lineage and *gibbôr ḥāyil*
- **Claim:** Narrative opens like 1 Sam 1:1 introducing the father with lineage. *gibbôr ḥāyil* (“a powerful person” / “man of substance”) refers to Kish (not Aphiah): originally military (“mighty warrior”), broadened to aristocrat/wealthy citizen; supported by head servant and donkeys (v. 3). Saul thus belongs to the ruling class though from a “junior clan of the smallest tribe” (v. 21).
- **Quote:** “The phrase a powerful person (gibbôr ḥāyil), or “a man of substance” (REB), would refer to “a member of the nobility,” especially of the “the warrior class, who became the landed aristocracy.” … Saul is thus a member of the ruling class even though he was from a “junior clan of the smallest tribe” (v. 21).”
- **Locus:** pp. 262–263 / L20–26; on 9:1
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R4-03 | Saul’s “goodness” and stature by human judgment
- **Claim:** *bāḥûr wāṭôb* is hendiadys “young and good”; *tôb* describes nature/personality more than mere looks (contrast Absalom’s *yāpeh*). “By human judgment Saul seemed to be the ideal person — fine and with a potential for anything, particularly as a leader.” Tallness (again 10:23) helped him impress; R. P. Gordon: “every inch a king.”
- **Quote:** “By human judgment Saul seemed to be the ideal person — fine and with a potential for anything, particularly as a leader whom the others would admire and follow.”
- **Locus:** p. 264 / L30–36; on 9:2
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R4-04 | Donkey search: ordinary incident, servant as head steward
- **Claim:** Lost donkeys were frequent (ANE parallel in Mari per Malamat) but rarely reported. *’aḥad mēhanne‘ārîm* likely “the head servant” (numeral “one” = “first”); *na‘ar* can mean steward/manager, not necessarily young; possibly even Ziba later. Nothing strange that a powerful man’s son went himself (C. H. Gordon compares Agamemnon seeking mules, *Iliad* 10:84).
- **Quote:** “Even though Saul was the son of a powerful man, there was nothing strange about his going on a donkey search himself.”
- **Locus:** pp. 264–266 / L52–60; on 9:3–4
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R4-05 | Servant’s intervention and providence
- **Claim:** When Saul would give up in the land of Zuph (Samuel’s district / Ramathaim), the servant makes “a critical intervention” with right information and the silver (v. 8) “at the right moment. The Lord was certainly engineering the circumstances behind all these matters.” “Man of God” = prophet; anonymity/ignorance may metonymically figure Saul’s unawareness of what lies ahead (R. P. Gordon).
- **Quote:** “Now is the time for the servant to speak up and make “a critical intervention”; he was able to give “the right information and the requisite item (v. 8)” at the right moment. The Lord was certainly engineering the circumstances behind all these matters.”
- **Locus:** pp. 267–268 / L120–128; on 9:5–6
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R4-06 | Gift (*tešûrāh*), “found” silver, and providential guidance
- **Claim:** *tešûrāh* (hapax) = gift of greeting (cf. Akk. *tāmartu* from *amāru* “see”); customary when seeking a seer’s help. Niphal *nimṣā’* (“here is found”) defocuses the agent — money “turned up almost miraculously”; “the narrative’s emphasis implies that the whole situation has been providentially guided by God. Now nothing can stand in the way of Saul’s meeting with Samuel.”
- **Quote:** “So, the money turned up almost miraculously. But the narrative’s emphasis implies that the whole situation has been providentially guided by God. Now “nothing can stand in the way of Saul’s meeting with Samuel.””
- **Locus:** pp. 269–270 / L132–138; on 9:7–8
- **Targets:** [[divine-providence]], [[saul]], [[samuel]]

### C-R4-07 | Gloss on “seer” (9:9) as literary insertion
- **Claim:** Against relocating v. 9 after 10 or 11, Tsumura takes it as deliberate “literary insertion” interrupting the dialogue cycle, slowing discourse and raising expectation; after the interruption Saul is reintroduced as primary agent. *rō’eh* outmoded to narrator but *nābî’* is ancient (Emar *nb’* 2nd millennium).
- **Quote:** “Another way of looking this unusual order would be to take it as a “literary insertion” … where the narrator deliberately inserted v. 9 into the dialogue pattern … to interrupt the flow of discourse and delay Saul’s response.”
- **Locus:** pp. 270–271 / L140–188; on 9:9
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R4-08 | Girls, feast, high place, timing of meeting
- **Claim:** Narrative tempo speeds with “Hurry now / just today / at this right moment.” Arrival “just in time” for feast where Saul will be guest of honour shows “overruling of providence.” High place (*bāmāh*) outside the wall; often negative in Deuteronomic theology, but “the present passage has no hint of a pagan connection … because of its association with Samuel.” Samuel’s main role at the feast is blessing the sacrifice (“grace”); slaughter by others.
- **Quote:** “Again the overruling of providence is evident, for the two travelers have arrived just in time for a feast at which, unaware of it as they are, Saul will be guest of honour.”
- **Locus:** pp. 271–273 / L204–218; on 9:11–14
- **Targets:** [[divine-providence]], [[samuel]], [[saul]]

### C-R4-09 | Lord’s prior revelation: anoint as *nāgîd*; Exodus echo; rule over people
- **Claim:** Disjunctive “Now, the Lord…” formally introduces the Lord as main agent; until now he “hidden behind the human events, engineering Saul’s circumstances.” Each step of the donkey search directed by the Lord. Anoint (*mšḥ*) marks transition/status; in Israel first a royal rite — king as Yahweh’s anointed/messiah. *nāgîd* first OT occurrence here: etymology unsettled (not necessarily passive *qatīl*); means “leader” of Yahweh’s people (not crown prince, since Kish not king); originally title of one designated by Yahweh or reigning monarch; might mean “regent” since God remains true king. Mission: deliver from Philistines; wording recalls Moses call (Exod 3:9). *ya‘ṣōr* “rule/govern” (not McCarter’s “muster”).
- **Quote:** “This section proves that the whole business of choosing Saul was by God’s will and guided by his providence. … Except for Samuel, nobody, including Saul, knew about God’s decision to choose Saul as prince over his people Israel.” / “Since God remained the true king, the title might well have meant “regent.””
- **Locus:** pp. 273–276 / L228–256; on 9:15–17
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[nāgîd]] (if used), [[divine-providence]], [[philistines]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R4-10 | Wordplay *ngd* / *nāgîd*; “longing of all Israel”
- **Claim:** Frequent Hi. *ngd* “tell” may wordplay on *nāgîd* (Shaviv), not primarily irony of ignorance (contra McCarter). Samuel contrasts donkeys with greater matters “in your heart.” *kol-ḥemdat yiśrā’ēl* via AXB pattern = “the longing of all Israel” — people’s desire for a king “like the nations” (8:5, 20); Saul to become focus of hopes against Philistine aggression (R. P. Gordon). Saul’s self-deprecation (Benjamin smallest tribe / humblest family) is traditional (Moses, Gideon) though Kish was actually powerful.
- **Quote:** “The expression the longing of all Israel … refers to the people’s desire … for a king “like all the (other) nations” in 1 Sam. 8:5, 20. Saul is to become a king just as all Israel longs for.”
- **Locus:** pp. 268–269, 276–278 / L128–132, L294–308; on 9:6–7, 18–21
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[philistines]]

### C-R4-11 | Banquet: reserved portion as royal/status symbolism
- **Claim:** Samuel could reserve portion because the Lord told him the day before; meal planned with ~30 regional representatives. Thigh etc. = tokens of new status (priest’s portion language). C. H. Gordon: “proportionate feast” (Homeric/ANE) marking rank. Meat kept for Saul “stands for the people” invited; eating with nobles at head seat signals support/subjugation. ANE: royal authority “depended largely on the goodwill and support of a powerful landowning and military aristocracy.” *mô‘ēd* “appointed time” recurs at Saul’s failure (13:8, 11).
- **Quote:** “This ritual symbolism of eating the special part of the meat reserved for Saul must have something to do with Saul’s ruling over the people (see 1 Sam. 9:17); for the thirty invited guests, who are probably the nobles of the region and represented the people, to eat with Saul at their head seat could mean their obedience and subjugation to him.”
- **Locus:** pp. 278–280 / L310–340; on 9:22–24
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]]

### C-R4-12 | Private anointing (10:1): *nāgîd* over Yahweh’s *naḥălāh*
- **Claim:** Private anointing (public lot-selection later, 10:17–27). Tsumura retains shorter MT against LXX long restoration (McCarter haplography claim: if haplography, why is *ky* preserved?). Oil on head: Emar high-priestess parallel. *naḥălāh* = Yahweh’s estate — land and people; Saul “vice-regent” over Lord’s estate; “Even though Israel has become a monarchy, it still is the Lord’s “estate,” and so Saul will be king only under God.”
- **Quote:** “Saul is now appointed or “designated” to lead or rule over Yahweh’s estate as his vice-regent. Even though Israel has become a monarchy, it still is the Lord’s “estate,” and so Saul will be king only under God.”
- **Locus:** pp. 281–282 / L374–396; on 10:1
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R4-13 | Predictive discourse grammar 10:2–8 vs narrative fulfillment 10:9–11
- **Claim:** 10:2–6 is “predictive discourse” dominated by *weqtl* (waw + perfect); narrative fulfillment (vv. 9–11) signaled by *wayqtl*. Three-part sign structure: two men (donkeys found) → three men (two loaves) → band of prophets + spirit rush. Bread gift = audience-gift / diplomatic acknowledgement of new royal authority (Wiseman); also priest’s share sacredness like 9:24 portion.
- **Quote:** “This section is a “predictive discourse” in which the verbal form qtl (perfect), preceded by waw, is dominant … as against wayqtl in a narrative discourse (see vv. 9–11).” / “9–11 This is an abbreviated account of the fulfillment of Samuel’s prediction … Note that the narrative discourse here is signaled by the wayqtl forms, while the predictive discourse is dominated by the weqtl forms.”
- **Locus:** pp. 283–284, 292 / L474–508, L620–624; on 10:2–11
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[saul]], [[samuel]]

### C-R4-14 | Signs geography: Rachel’s tomb, Gibeath-elohim, Philistine garrisons
- **Claim:** Rachel’s tomb location debated; Tsumura: original near Ramah on Bethlehem/Ephrath road; modern site later tradition. Zelzah only here; unusual word order as AXB literary insertion, not McCarter’s LXX conjecture. Gibeath-elohim / Gibeah ≈ Gibeah of Saul (Tell el-Fûl). Philistine garrisons (*neṣībê*) plural = composite fortresses; mentioned because Saul will be empowered to deliver from them. Fortress I at Tell el-Fûl variously Saul’s or Philistine (Albright vs Alt/Mazar).
- **Quote:** “The reason why Philistine garrisons is mentioned here is probably that Saul would be empowered by God to deliver his people from them.”
- **Locus:** pp. 284–286 / L510–528; on 10:2–5
- **Targets:** [[philistines]], [[saul]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R4-15 | Band of prophets, spirit rush, “another person”
- **Claim:** *ḥebel nebî’îm* more like Mari *āpilum* groups than *muḫḫûm* ecstasy; text stresses group prophesying with instruments under spirit of the Lord, not pagan self-mutilation. Israelite prophecy not mere outgrowth of Canaanite ecstatic prophecy. *rûaḥ YHWH* in Samuel only with Yahweh’s anointed (Saul/David); *ṣlḥ* + spirit in Samson/Saul/David stories. Spirit equips for service / dispels doubts / public demonstration as prince; “Saul’s possession has to do with his election, not with his becoming a prophet” (Wilson). *’îš ’aḥēr* / later *lēb ’aḥēr* = new role-power, not loss of self.
- **Quote:** “Thus, the spirit of Yahweh was given to His anointed that they might fulfill their responsibility as the representative of the people Israel and as the vice-regent of God.” / “To change to another person … is not necessarily becoming another person by losing oneself, but rather by being equipped with power to play a new role”
- **Locus:** pp. 286–288 / L530–540; on 10:5–6, 9
- **Targets:** [[saul]], [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R4-16 | “Do what your hand finds”; God with you; Gilgal wait (10:7–8)
- **Claim:** Three signs: two men, two loaves, spirit. “What your hand finds” = ability/opportunity (Ammonite crisis or Philistine challenge), not impulse surrender (contra McCarter). “God will be with you” said of Saul only this once vs many times for David. V. 8 not merely secondary prep for ch. 13: imperative-force *weqtl*; visit within weeks/months before Mizpah assembly (10:17); Gilgal also site of official kingship (11:15). “Wait seven days” may mean religious “wait on God” / seven-day retreat/Sabbath-related off-duty (LXX *dialeipseis*; Ugar. *ḥl* cultic clearance), not only clock-waiting for Samuel. Full relationship to 13:7b–15 deferred to ch. 13.
- **Quote:** “Saul can do whatever his hand finds to do because of God’s presence with him. But there is one thing he should do before he goes out and fulfills his role as Yahweh’s anointed.” / “It may be reasonably conjectured that Saul was ordered “to make a seven-day retreat” before becoming engaged in any kingly activity.”
- **Locus:** pp. 288–291 / L544–586; on 10:7–8

### C-R4-17 | “Is Saul among the prophets?” proverb
- **Claim:** Neighbors’ proverb given original setting here; reappears 19:24 with different/negative nuance. Need not express negative evaluation of Saul or prophets (R. P. Gordon); modern readers can only guess meaning (McCarter). “Who is their father?” not hereditary office; “father” may = professional leader (Elijah/Elisha), not Saul as their leader. After prophesying Saul “came back to the hill” (*habbāmāh* here older non-religious “hill” = home area, not private high-place devotion).

- **Claim:** Uncle (probably Abner) questions; Saul reports donkeys found but “of the matter of the monarchy (*melûkāh*) of which Samuel had spoken he told him nothing.” Same term anticipates *mišpaṭ hammelūkāh* (v. 25). Secret until public Mizpah declaration (R. P. Gordon).

### C-R4-19 | Mizpah public election: lot, hiding, acclamation
- **Claim:** Assembly responds to ch. 8 demand; shows Saul is God’s choice not only Samuel’s. Prophetic speech: deliverance from Egypt vs people’s rejection of God who saves. Lot elimination (tribe→clan Matri→Saul); structure PEOPLE–TRIBE–CLAN–FAMILY. Further inquiry to Lord (not same lot method) finds Saul hiding by baggage — not mere shyness but fear of “new and responsible position.” Tallness again crucial to people. First time since 9:1f Saul called “king” — “significantly, it is the people who acclaim him so” (R. P. Gordon). “Lord has chosen” (Samuel) vs later “you have chosen” (12:13).
- **Quote:** “At last Saul is publicly and officially presented and accepted by the people as the king. … “for the first time since his introduction in 9:1f. Saul is called ‘king’; significantly, it is the people who acclaim him so.””
- **Locus:** pp. 296–299 / L804–834; on 10:17–24

### C-R4-20 | *mišpaṭ hammelūkāh*: written constitution before the Lord
- **Claim:** Samuel’s tripartite legal action: announced, wrote, laid before the Lord (deposited in sanctuary; cf. covenant document / book of the law by ark). Samuel intermediary/witness between king and people. *mišpaṭ hammelūkāh* = rules of the institution/relationship between king and people (not identical to *mišpaṭ hammelek* “right of the king” in 8:9, 11; more specific than Deut 17:18 “this law”). Samuel still main authority figure. Contrast Deut 17:18.
- **Quote:** “Since the right of the king (mišpaṭ hammelek) had been publicly announced by Samuel in 8:9, 11, the rules (mišpaṭ) here must be rather on the institution of monarchy, that is, the relationship between the king and the people, concerning which both the newly enthroned king and the people must have “legal” agreement.”
- **Locus:** pp. 299–300 / L836–844; on 10:25

### C-R4-21 | King de jure vs de facto; silence; supporters and “worthless men”
- **Claim:** Saul returns to Gibeah and normal work; “only king de jure” until he proves himself (Wellhausen); de facto after military proof (11:15). Band whose hearts God touched support him; worthless men despise and withhold gift. MT *kemaḥărîš* “as one who keeps silent” retained vs 4QSamᵃ/Cross “About a month later” — Herbert: 4QSamᵃ reading “originally absent”; MT explains personality and prepares next stage.
- **Quote:** “So, as Wellhausen notes, “Saul is at this point only king de jure; he does not become king de facto until after he has proved himself.”” / “The MT reading And he was as one who keeps silent explains the personality of Saul well and prepares the audience for the next stage of this drama with expectation.”

### C-R4-22 | Ch. 11: transition; limited monarchy; historical reliability
- **Claim:** Ch. 11 transitions from Samuel’s judgeship to Saul’s kingship; Saul still needs Samuel’s authority for mobilization; Samuel summons Gilgal renewal. Purpose of 11:1–13: show Saul “king de facto” with loyalty of all Israel, yet “limited monarchy” requiring popular acceptance. Generally accepted as “a reliable historical source.” Embraced by Mizpah election and Gilgal coronation.
- **Quote:** “The purpose of this episode is “to show that Saul … has now become king de facto and earned the loyalty of all Israel.” However, Saul’s kingship is a “limited monarchy” since acceptance by the people is necessary.”

### C-R4-23 | Nahash, Jabesh, 4QSamᵃ plus; premonarchic federation
- **Claim:** Tsumura does not adopt NRSV/4QSamᵃ long plus before 11:1 as necessarily original MT loss (no haplography trigger; “king of Ammonites” phrasing twice in plus looks secondary from 12:12; possible multiple versions). wayya‘al motion-verb = transition SETTING, not gap signal. Jabesh can cut own international treaty — independence within loose tribal federation; Nahash’s “reproach against all Israel” shows knowledge of federation and intent to challenge all Israel. *bezō’t* = “by this means” (gouging right eyes as treaty means, not mere condition). Seven-day wait = calculated policy; *môšîa‘* echoes judges deliverers.
- **Quote:** “The biblical narrator is concerned more with the delivery of the Transjordan Israelites by Saul than with their oppression by Nahash, king of the Ammonites. The demand for a king to rule over them in ch. 8 might have been made in the midst of this Ammonite oppression; see on 12:12.”

### C-R4-24 | Spirit, oxen curse, mustering, victory, de facto kingship
- **Claim:** Saul still plowing after Mizpah (king elect). Spirit rush (same phrase as 10:6) yields martial anger/power like Samson/judges — more charismatic judge than constitutional monarch, yet act presupposes authority. Dismembered oxen = conditional curse; “Saul and Samuel” invokes Samuel’s authority (Ishida: not secondary). *paḥad YHWH* falls on Israel for victory (not only on enemies). Numbers MT 300k+30k preferred as smaller. Three divisions / morning watch. 11:12–13 brackets 10:27 worthless men; victory establishes kingship; Saul forbids blood revenge — “the Lord made a victory.” Saul becomes king de facto.

### C-R4-25 | Gilgal: renew kingship — political vs religious dimensions
- **Claim:** Samuel the “king-maker” summons to Gilgal (cf. 10:8 wait; later ch. 15 rejection site). “Renew the kingship” not re-grant after Mizpah acclamation; for Tsumura, renewal concerns confirming Saul before the Lord and (with Vannoy-leaning note) allegiance to Yahweh’s kingship; not mere editorial harmonization. If Mizpah political, Gilgal religious confirmation. Elaborate “Gilgal / before the Lord” repetition = TERMINUS; 12:1 starts new episode (wayyo’mer + subject). Peace offerings shared feast; Samuel present though unnamed. Celebration of Ammonite victory and new monarchy; whether covenant-ratification needs ch. 12 decision.
- **Quote:** “If the election of Saul as king at Mizpah was political, the (re)confirmation of Saul as the king at Gilgal would be religious, that is, before the Lord. ### C-R4-26 | Ch. 12 frame: watershed; not simply “farewell” or pure covenant form
- **Claim:** Ch. 12 is watershed judges→kingship; thematically/literarily corresponds to ch. 8; people first recognize evil of asking for king (v. 19) but “too late.” Often compared to Joshua 24 as Deuteronomic covenant renewal (Muilenburg, Weiser, McCarthy, Baltzer, Birch, Vannoy, McCarter). Vannoy: full covenant-renewal form (history, challenge, blessing/curse, theophanic sign); 11:14–12:25 dual purpose continuity + restoration. Tsumura (with Knutson’s caution): formal similarities exist, but main thrust is Samuel’s “negative confession” / justifying past conduct before Lord and people (witness formula v. 5 about Samuel–people, not primarily God–people covenant). Not so much “formal initiation of prophet’s new role” (McCarter) as change of political leadership; Samuel drops judgeship duties, continues as prophet (intercession/instruction) and future king-maker for “a greater king than Saul.” Not accurately a retirement/farewell address.
- **Quote:** “Despite the formal similarities with covenants, the purpose of the present chapter is to convey Samuel’s new role and his relationship with the people rather than God’s covenantal relationship with the people.” / “While Samuel just drops his duties with respect to judgeship, his prophetic duties remain the same.” / “it is not accurate to call the present speech the “farewell address” of Samuel.”
- **Locus:** pp. 314–316 / L1074–1088; intro to 12:1–25
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[1-samuel]], [[saul]]

### C-R4-27 | Negative confession; walk before; anointed as witness
- **Claim:** wayyō’mer + subject begins new episode; sparse narrative framework — possibly not during Gilgal ceremony; more likely different occasion, possibly Ramah (echo 8:22). “Walk before” = perform function on someone’s behalf; king vs Samuel contrasted. Legal “Testify against me” protests deposition though leadership just. Conditional sentence with parenthetical questions (AXB). King as “chief justiciary.” Ox/donkey = representative possessions; Hittite Puḫanu parallel for negative confession. Defraud/oppress pair and bribe (*kōper*) contrast Samuel with his sons (8:3), not primarily with royal “take” list (8:11–17). Blinded eyes = ignore truth (bribe blinds). People affirm; Lord and anointed as witnesses (AXBY pattern); third-person formula declaration. Samuel invokes Lord who appointed Moses and Aaron — implicit comparison as deliverer; anointed dropped as witness in v. 6.
- **Quote:** “With this legal expression Samuel “protests against his deposition by the people on the grounds that his leadership has been just.”” / “Samuel contrasts himself with his sons rather than with the king.”
- **Locus:** pp. 316–320 / L1088–1188; on 12:1–6
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[monarchy-request]]

### C-R4-28 | Historical résumé 12:7–12; Nahash motive for king-request
- **Claim:** *we‘attāh* starts unit; discourse unit is vv. 7–12 résumé (not Noth’s Deuteronomistic 6–15 insert as such). Salvation-history summary like Ps 78 / Acts 13. Juridical “take your stand”; Niphal “argue my case” — Samuel prosecutor and self-trial. *ṣidqôt YHWH* = righteous acts including disciplinary (v. 9). Judges pattern miniaturized (forgot–cried–sent–delivered). Bedan possibly phonetic variant of Barak; MT/LXX “Samuel” self-naming retained (not emend to Samson). Nahash reference links ch. 11 and suggests demand for king (8:5) responded to Ammonite threat (possibly longstanding; 4QSamᵃ/Josephus if true strengthen this). “Though the Lord your God was your king.”
- **Quote:** “The reference to Nahash, the king of the Ammonites, reminds us of the incident in ch. 11 and gives the impression that the demand for a king in 8:5 was a response to the new threat posed by Nahash the Ammonite in 11:1. However, the threat may have existed for some time before Nahash’s attack on Jabash-gilead.”
- **Locus:** pp. 320–323 / L1190–1308; on 12:7–12
- **Targets:** [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R4-29 | Conditional covenant language 12:13–15: fear/serve/listen; king under law
- **Claim:** “Here is the king whom you have chosen… the Lord has set” — no need to force Mizpah or Gilgal setting; with v. 2 implies king already ruling some time. “You have chosen” need not be more negative than 10:24 “Lord has chosen” — Lord *nātan* the king. Vv. 14–15 ≈ blessing/curse; stipulations like Deut 12–26; Josh 24:14. Triple: fear, serve, listen; no disobedience to Lord’s mouth. **Both people and king** must follow the Lord — king not exempt. Apodosis of 14 not missing “it will be well” (against many modern versions): if you (claim to) fear…, both you and the king who rules over you will be following the Lord. Disobedience → hand of Lord on “entire household” (*you and your fathers* as household idiom, not dead fathers / not McCarter’s “king to destroy you”).
- **Quote:** “Not only the people but also the king should be obedient to the Lord; no king in Israel is exempted from obeying the Lord’s commandments.” / “what the apodosis intends to convey is clear: even the king who rules over you is not exempt from obeying the divine law.”
- **Locus:** pp. 323–324 / L1308–1322; on 12:13–15
- **Targets:** [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[monarchy-request]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R4-30 | Rain/thunder sign at wheat harvest (12:16–19)
- **Claim:** Wheat harvest May–June — rain rare; thunder/rain = supernatural sign via prophet. Purpose (v. 17): people know evil of asking for king is great in Lord’s eyes (not mainly McCarter’s prophet–Lord bond display; not forced Longman/Vannoy “covenant curse on crop”). Ugaritic *ytn ql* Baal’s thunder vs Yahweh creator expressing through nature. Syntax of “evil… great in Lord’s eyes by asking for a king” via vertical grammar / AX//BY overlap. People fear Lord and Samuel greatly; ask intercession — first true humility vs 8:5 attitude; Moses parallel; “not a retirement ceremony.”
- **Quote:** “Verse 17 explains that its purpose is that the people know that their evil is great in the Lord’s eyes.” / “To be sure, this is not “a retirement ceremony” for Samuel; his authority as prophet remains powerful.”
- **Locus:** pp. 324–327 / L1324–1450; on 12:16–19
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R4-31 | Final admonition 12:20–25: fear/serve; idols *tōhû*; prayer/teach; shared fate
- **Claim:** Emphatic pronouns contrast people and prophet: asking for king = people’s “evil”; ceasing to pray = prophet’s potential “sin.” Particle *’ak* (only) frames central message: fear and serve Lord with all heart (vv. 20, 24 inclusio). Do not turn to *tōhû* vain idols (“emptiness/nothing”). Lord will not forsake people because of his great name / willingness to make them his people (grace principle). Samuel’s ongoing roles: intercession and instruction (“way to the good and right thing”). V. 25: if act wickedly, **both you and your king** swept away — fate of king one with people (cf. v. 14). Prepares narrative for Saul’s rejection for disobedience in following chapters.
- **Quote:** “Note that the fate of the king in Israel is one with that of the people (both you and your king; see also v. 14). Both the people and the king are obliged to obey the word of the Lord or else both of them will be swept away. Because of disobedience to the word of the Lord, Saul will be rejected from being king over Israel in the following chapter.”
- **Locus:** pp. 327–330 / L1404–1486; on 12:20–25
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R4-32 | ANE royal ideology comparisons (scattered in range)
- **Claim:** Tsumura repeatedly situates motifs in ANE/Homeric frames without equating theologies: Mari donkey-search report; gift/greeting customs (Akk. *tāmartu*; Odyssey gifts); proportionate feast (Odyssey/Iliad; Gen 43:34); anointing status transitions (Fleming; Emar priestess oil); *nāgîd* as military commander proving worth (Nebuchadnezzar parallel for crown-prince battle proof); Mari *āpilum* prophetic groups; Saul’s tallness vs Athtar in Baal myth (height motif, different criteria); kingship needing aristocratic support; Hittite negative confession (Puḫanu); Baal *ytn ql* vs Yahweh thunder; Mesha/Mari three-company tactics. Distinctive Israelite note: high place without pagan charge under Samuel; peace offerings vs Ugaritic *šlmm* different significance for monotheism; king only under God / regent over Lord’s estate.
- **Quote:** “As is often the case in the ancient Near East, in spite of his claim to divine endorsement, the “authority [of a king] depended largely on the goodwill and support of a powerful landowning and military aristocracy.”” / “Even though Israel has become a monarchy, it still is the Lord’s “estate,” and so Saul will be king only under God.”
- **Locus:** various: pp. 265–66, 269, 274–75, 279–80, 282, 286–87, 298, 318–19, 325 / throughout 9–12
- **Targets:** [[kingship-in-israel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[1-samuel]]
